doc.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010

title: Woody Herman and Buddy Rich lessons
summary: LaLama's first top-level gig was Woody Herman, where he learned a leader must trust you; on Buddy Rich he tells how Rich fired an untalented trumpet section.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Well I can’t, that’s a hard — here I could explain it in a certain way. My first band was Woody Herman and that was like my first professional jazz gig so to speak. I mean I’d played a lot of gigs, but I don’t mean professional as far as getting paid, but upper eschelons jazz. And Woody, and I just learned a lot. I learned a lot from Woody because of the fact that I finally realized that a leader has to trust you. I don’t mean just showing up on time, but the music and showing up on time, and just being there for the gig. That’s when he starts liking you, when he trusts you. And that was a big lesson. I mean it just hit me one day, oh man, that’s how you get along.
To trust you to not only play but —

Be there, and you know, just be there. But even the music too. I mean musically he has to trust you. When you go up to play, let’s say a solo, you’re going to be right. You know? I’m not saying you can’t make a mistake, I mean it’s just the attitude. And okay, and then I went to Buddy Rich and I really enjoyed that too. Well Buddy was a lunatic but still he was a real musician. I’m not totally agreeable when I hear all these stories. Not that they weren’t true, but his attitude really wasn’t like — he was a musician, you know what I mean? And he wanted things right. I can tell you a couple of stories. I remember one time the whole trumpet section was gone and they hired all these guys from North Texas State. And they really weren’t up to snuff. I mean they couldn’t handle — and we all figured oh Buddy, he’s going to go crazy. He didn’t say a word. He just fired them. He gave them their two weeks notice. You know why? Because he knew they weren’t that talented. But he would holler at you if he knew you were talented and you weren’t doing the job, you know? So I respected him. You know what I mean? And I remember another time he invited Mel Lewis to the band because he couldn’t even get dressed, he had this back problem with his discs. He couldn’t get dressed, right? So I remember they had to help him get dressed. He would get dressed on the bus. But I remember Mel was there for a week but didn’t play one beat. Because Buddy would, after all that pain — I mean I saw this guy was in pain. You know when somebody is in pain, they’re not faking it you know. So he would go up there and play. And then he’d go back, and he was in pain. So he had Mel Lewis there, but Mel didn’t play a note. Okay now in London I ended up, we were there for a month, we were at Ronnie Scott’s for a week but I got sick, I had the flu, I had to go to the doctor, you know, I mean I had a 103 temperature. I had a terrible flu. And Steve Marcus and Andy Fusco went into Buddy’s room and said, “Buddy, man, Ralph is sick, I mean I don’t know if he can play.” And he goes, “Is he dead?” They said, “No.” And then so I’m on the bandstand and I played and I think he called almost every tune I played on too.
